claims.text: Decomp-toolkit automates function, section and relocation analysis and splits per user configuration, but its own docs say relocation output needs 'manual tweaking' in data. The community splitting guide treats carving a big executable into original source files as a manual, widely disliked but essential step, so the project schedule should budget for it.

meta.query: What evidence shows that the translation-unit boundaries and section splits a decompilation tool proposes automatically for a GameCube or Wii executable differ from the original compilation units, and how often do projects have to correct them by hand?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming automated splitting delivers finished file boundaries and plan for a human-driven stage of boundary-finding before real decompilation work can begin.

claims.text: Practitioners locate original file boundaries from compiler artifacts: each file has at most one static-initialization function, and duplicate float constants approximately mark a boundary because the compiler dedupes them only per file. The guide calls these hints approximate and notes exceptions (files without an initializer, weak functions kept globally), so they are leads to confirm, not authoritative splits.

claims.text: When two components supply the same default behavior and both are marked as replaceable, the linker silently keeps whichever it sees first and drops the other with no warning. Merely swapping two file names in the build list produced a program that printed something different, so the shipped product's behavior can change without any code edit or error.

claims.text: If two parts of a codebase accidentally define a same-named helper differently, the toolchain assumes they are identical and keeps one without complaint. In the demonstrated case the winner flipped with file order and with optimization level, so a bug can show up in Debug builds, vanish in Release, and return when someone reorders sources. Even link-time checking tools reported nothing.

claims.text: The safe pattern is one replaceable default with one firm override, because a firm definition always beats a replaceable one and two firm definitions stop the build. Risk appears when two components each provide a replaceable override, or when libraries are bundled in archives, where the first library listed supplies the function and the duplicate in the second is never examined, so no error appears.

meta.capability: You can require that vendor or third-party packages ship exactly one replaceable default plus one firm override per feature, so a duplicate becomes a loud build failure rather than a silent product-behavior choice.

claims.text: In the Hex-Rays example, one wrong stack adjustment after a single call (the callee actually used a register, not stack arguments) produced wrong values downstream. The fix was to correct that one place, or the shared function's properties if many callers were affected. Errors from one bad assumption propagate, but they can be traced back to the first point where values diverge and repaired there.

claims.text: Reverse-engineering practice relies on invariants, such as values matching at both ends of a jump and returning to zero at function exit, to expose errors at the first point of divergence. Equivalent invariants at file boundaries would flag a misplaced split near the point it happens rather than far later. The tooling also warns that a wrong type can wreak havoc easily, so errors tend to surface far from their cause.

The vendor itself says that having symbols does not guarantee correct results, which is why override options exist. Inferring original file order and object boundaries from a final binary therefore cannot rest on these sources and needs Metrowerks-specific linker maps or reverse-engineering notes.

claims.text: Because a linker merges same-type segments from every object file into one segment per type, the final binary groups code and data by kind, not by the source file that contributed them. Object boundaries inside a merged section must therefore be recovered from other cues such as alignment gaps or symbol order, not from the section layout alone.

claims.text: A merging tool that combines all of a project's C files into one renames conflicting file-local names with a numeric suffix and removes duplicate global declarations that came from shared headers. It also coalesces same-named structures and types, using different names where they aren't identical. The merged output therefore no longer maps one-to-one onto the original files, which is the mechanism by which a merge becomes hard to see from the result alone.

meta.capability: You can stop assuming a combined whole-program build is a plain concatenation, and instead expect that merging sources silently renames and collapses code, so what the merged result shows will differ from what the individual files contained.

claims.text: The merger works by posing as the compiler and linker, saving preprocessed source under each object file's name, and then combining those at link time. It states that the merge flag must be used throughout the build process and that compile and link arguments must be identical for all files. A mixed build, or one with differing arguments, would therefore give incomplete or inconsistent merged results.

meta.capability: You can require that any whole-program analysis be run on a build where every step went through the merging tool, rather than trusting a partial or mixed build.

claims.text: When source and the shipped package diverge, the shipped binary is the system of record, so approval should fail until the artifact is independently validated. Even a signed binary that the source cannot reproduce is not trustworthy on the signature alone. For a reconstruction whose split links and matches the original, this implies a successful match proves only the output, not that the boundaries are right.

claims.text: Teams typically learn of mismatches or boundary failures only after the damage is done, such as an extension already touching tokens or an odd filename already accepted in production, rather than through planned review. The corrective is intentional negative testing and rebuild-and-diff in a clean environment, comparing what was decided with what actually happens. A wrong file split that links fine would likewise surface late, unless someone deliberately tests it.

claims.text: The linker merges byte-identical functions into one copy by default in release builds, so a crash trace can name a different function than the one that ran, and breakpoints may be impossible to set. Debug builds switch this off by default, so the team debugging a problem and the shipped product can show different structure. The program's behavior is unchanged; only the diagnostic picture is distorted.

meta.query: Why does an optimizing compiler or linker remove the gaps between neighboring functions and merge identical constants, so that a single source file looks like several or several files look like one?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming that a debugger or crash report showing one function name reflects the real code path, and decide to keep the size-saving merge off in builds used for diagnosing problems.

claims.text: Merging identical functions or read-only data gives different items the same address, which can break software that relies on unique addresses. GCC's more aggressive constant-merging mode is explicitly non-conforming to the C and C++ language rules, while the default constant merging is on for optimized builds. The size and speed gains must be weighed against this compatibility risk, mostly for unusual or low-level code.

claims.text: Another project, Total Annihilation, reached 100% of 3,267 functions and a full rebuild whose MD5 matches the shipped exe, but only by placing each function and data item at its original address. An ordinary linker run produces different bytes because functions land where the linker puts them. Matching individual functions therefore does not recover the original link order, and a byte-identical build can depend on forced placement rather than on a recovered layout.
